title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Obj. 3 Solut close: Regeneration and election govern actual efficacy
pass_a_gloss: In this argument a false supposition is wrapped up. For in the major proposition it is taken as conceded that the efficacy or virtue of some cause is always to be estimated greater or lesser according as it extends itself to more or fewer subjects: which is most false. For a cause's efficacy or excellence is to be estimated from the very nature and excellence of the effects rather than from multitude. For example, it is an argument of greater virtue and excellence if someone restores eyes to one blind human than if he digs out eyes from a thousand; if he heals one mutilated and sick person than if he mutilates or poisons a thousand healthy and whole humans; in a word, if he recalls one human to life than if he gives a thousand over to slaughter. By equal reason greater and more efficacious is the force of Christ saving even one human by his death than of Adam destroying the whole human race by his sin. To the Minor also it can be answered that the very act of Adam sinning does not bind any human with death's guilt or render him liable to Divine wrath except insofar as he is propagated from Adam sinning by natural generation: and in the same way exactly the act of Christ dying does not snatch any human out of the state of death nor free him from Divine wrath except insofar as he is derived from Christ by supernatural regeneration. On both sides therefore the condition is equal if a just comparison is instituted. All generated from Adam naturally lost God's grace and life: All regenerated from Christ supernaturally recover God's grace and life. No one by the fault of Adam sinning is subjected to death or Divine wrath unless he has drawn natural origin from him: No one by the merit of Christ dying is exempted from death or Divine wrath unless he has drawn heavenly birth from him. Prudently and learnedly this is explained by Aquinas, Contra Gentiles book 4 chapter 55, where he has this: The effect of the first parent's sin reaches each one through origin of the flesh; so the effect of Christ's death reaches each one through spiritual regeneration. It is necessary that he who desires Christ's merit to work in himself be regenerated by Christ's Spirit. If someone still presses, To be propagated from Adam, whence wrath and death's guilt follow, is common to all humans; why is to be regenerated through Christ, whence our reconciliation and salvation depend, not established as common to all in the same way? Nothing else is there for me to answer than that God himself did not will that those things which flow to humans by way of grace should be common to all in the same way as those things are which are derived to humans by way of nature. He willed his grace to distinguish humans from humans, and therefore did not will to make it equally common to all humans. Augustine noted this, On the Predestination of the Saints chapter 5; inspect him at leisure. Let no one therefore murmur against God that by the operation of special grace he regenerates certain ones and inserts them into Christ through faith; let no one ask why he frees that one rather than this: because to stop the mouths of any and all this reply of God himself suffices (Matthew 20:15): Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine? etc.; that of the Apostle (Romans 9:18): He has mercy on whom he wills. See also Augustine, On the Good of Perseverance chapter 8. Although therefore as to the sufficiency of Christ's death it relates equally to all, yet as to efficacy it depends on Divine election, that the effects of Christ's merits are mercifully applied to certain ones while by their own unbelief impeding they are not applied to others. Thus far answer has been given to those who fight for the universal and likewise actual reconciliation of all and singular humans: Now let us hear what can be brought forward by those who state that the elect themselves by the efficacy of Christ's death have been justified from eternity and reconciled to God.
pass_b_english: This argument smuggles in a false assumption. Its major premise treats it as conceded that the efficacy or virtue of a cause is always to be rated greater or lesser according as it reaches more or fewer subjects. That is quite false. A cause's efficacy—or excellence—must be judged from the nature and excellence of its effects, not from how many subjects it touches. Restoring sight to one blind person shows greater virtue than gouging out the eyes of a thousand; healing one mutilated and sick person shows more than mutilating or poisoning a thousand who are healthy and whole; in a word, recalling one human being to life shows more than handing a thousand over to slaughter. By the same measure, Christ's power in saving even one human being by his death is greater and more efficacious than Adam's power in destroying the whole human race by his sin.

To the minor premise one may also reply that Adam's very act of sinning binds no one with the guilt of death, and makes no one liable to divine wrath, except insofar as that person is propagated from sinful Adam by natural generation. In exactly the same way, Christ's dying act snatches no one out of the state of death, and frees no one from divine wrath, except insofar as that person is derived from Christ by supernatural regeneration. On both sides, then, the condition is equal if the comparison is just. All who are generated from Adam by nature lost God's grace and life; all who are regenerated from Christ by grace recover God's grace and life. No one is subjected to death or divine wrath by Adam's fault unless he has drawn natural origin from Adam; no one is exempted from death or divine wrath by Christ's merit unless he has drawn heavenly birth from Christ.

Aquinas explains this prudently and learnedly in Against the Gentiles, book 4, chapter 55: the effect of the first parent's sin reaches each person through the origin of the flesh; so the effect of Christ's death reaches each through spiritual regeneration. Anyone who wants Christ's merit to work in himself must be regenerated by Christ's Spirit. If someone still presses the point—propagation from Adam, from which wrath and the guilt of death follow, is common to all; why then is regeneration through Christ, on which our reconciliation and salvation depend, not made common to all in the same way?—I have nothing else to answer than this: God himself did not will that what flows to human beings by way of grace should be common to all in the same way as what comes by way of nature. He willed his grace to distinguish one person from another, and therefore did not will to make it equally common to all. Augustine noted this in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 5; read him at leisure. Let no one murmur against God, then, because by the working of special grace he regenerates some and grafts them into Christ through faith; let no one ask why he frees that one rather than this. To stop every mouth it is enough that God himself answers (Matthew 20:15), "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine?" and so on; and that the Apostle says (Romans 9:18), "He has mercy on whom he wills." See also Augustine, On the Good of Perseverance, chapter 8. So although, as to sufficiency, Christ's death stands equally related to all, as to efficacy it depends on divine election: the effects of Christ's merits are mercifully applied to some, while others, hindered by their own unbelief, do not receive that application.

So far we have answered those who contend for a universal and likewise actual reconciliation of all human beings, each and every one. Now let us hear what can be urged by those who hold that the elect themselves, by the efficacy of Christ's death, were justified from eternity and reconciled to God.
source_text:
In hoc argumento involvitur falsa suppositio. In majore enim propositione quasi pro concesso sumitur, Efficaciam sive virtutem causae alicujus majorem semper aut minorem aestimandam, prout ad plura aut pauciora subjecta sese extendat: quod falsissimum est. Aestimanda enim est causae efficacia, sive excellentia, ex natura ipsa & excellentia effectorum, potius quam ex multitudine. Exempli causa, majoris virtutis atque excellentiae argumentum est, si quis uni homini caeco oculos restituat, quam si mille hominibus oculos effodiat; si unicum mutilatum & morbidum sanet, quam si mille homines sanos & integros mutiliet, aut veneno inficiat; uno verbo, si unum hominem ad vitam revocet, quam si mille neci dederit. Pari ratione major & efficacior est vis Christi morte sua vel unum hominem servantis, quam Adami peccato suo totum humanum genus perdentis. Ad Minorem etiam responderi potest, ipsum actum Adami peccantis non constringere ullum hominem reatu mortis, aut obnoxium reddere irae Divinae, nisi exinde quod ab Adamo peccante per generationem naturalem propagetur: atque ad eundem plane modum actus Christi morientis non eripit ullum hominem e statu mortis, neque ab ira Divina liberat, nisi in quantum a Christo per regenerationem supernaturalem derivetur. Utrobique igitur par conditio, si instituatur justa comparatio. Omnes ab Adamo generati naturaliter gratiam Dei ac vitam perdiderunt: Omnes a Christo regenerati supernaturaliter gratiam Dei ac vitam recuperant. Nullus vitio Adami peccantis morti aut irae Divinae subjicitur, nisi ab eo traxerit originem naturalem: Nullus merito Christi morientis a morte aut ira Divina eximitur, nisi ab eo traxerit caelestem nativitatem. Prudenter & docte hoc ab Aquinate explicatur, Contra Gentil. lib. 4. cap. 55. ubi haec habet, Effectus peccati primi parentis pervenit ad unumquemque per carnis originem: sic effectus mortis Christi pertingit ad unumquemque per spiritualem regenerationem. Oportet per Christi Spiritum regenerari, qui cupit Christi meritum in se operari. Si quis adhuc urgeat, Ab Adamo propagari, unde ira consequitur & mortis reatus, est hominibus universis commune; cur per Christum regenerari, unde dependet reconciliatio & salus nostra, non eodem modo omnibus commune statuitur? Nihil aliud est quod respondeam quam, Deum ipsum noluisse, ea quae per modum gratiae ad homines fluunt, ita esse communia omnibus, atque sunt ea quae per modum naturae ad homines derivantur. Voluit gratiam suam discernere homines ab hominibus, ac proinde noluit eam ex aequo communem facere omnibus hominibus. Notavit hoc Augustinus, De Praedest. Sanctor. cap. 5. quem per otium inspicite. Nemo igitur contra Deum obmurmuret, quod specialis gratiae operatione quosdam regeneret, & per fidem in Christum inserat; nemo quaerat cur illum potius quam hunc liberet: quia ad obstuenda ora quorumcunque sufficit hic illud responsum ipsius Dei, Matth. xx. 15. Licet mihi de meo facere quod volo, &c. illud Apostoli, Rom. ix. 18. Misereatur cujus vult. Videte etiam Augustinum, De bono persev. c. 8. Quamvis igitur quantum ad sufficientiam mortis Christi aequaliter se habeat ad omnes, tamen quantum ad efficaciam ex Divina electione pendet, quod effectus meritorum Christi quibusdam misericorditer applicentur, dum propria sua infidelitate impediente aliis non applicentur.

Hactenus responsum est illis qui pugnant pro universali eademque actuali omnium & singulorum hominum reconciliatione: Jam audiamus quid ab illis afferri possit, qui electos ipsos efficacia mortis Christi ab aeterno justificatos, & Deo reconciliatos, statuunt.
